name: Economic democracy
summary: Economic democracy extends democratic control into the economy: firms are governed by their workers one person one vote, and investment is steered by public bodies rather than private savers. It keeps markets for goods and services but replaces labor and capital markets with worker self-management and publicly financed investment. Its aim is to end capitalism's democratic deficits and structural unemployment without central planning.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: Schweickart's basic model replaces most wage labour with cooperative labour while keeping a small capitalist sector (s6), and Ellerman holds that the inalienability argument implies abolishing wage labour in favour of universal self-employment (s9, Chapter 4).

automate-paid-work.rationale: Schweickart says workers in a democratic firm can take productivity gains from new technology as leisure rather than income, and that Keynes's fifteen-hour week could be reached under Economic Democracy (s6).

ban-interest.rationale: Schweickart's socialist savings and loan associations pay interest to savers and charge interest on consumer loans (s6), though investment finance is not interest-based.

basic-income.rationale: Malleson's picture of economic democracy has high taxation paying for excellent public services, 'perhaps a Guaranteed Basic Income' (s7), which is a hedged endorsement.

capital-controls.rationale: Schweickart says investment funds are publicly raised and required by law to be reinvested in domestic firms, so that capital is not exported and foreign capital does not flow in (s6, section on socialist protectionism).

central-planning.rationale: Schweickart rejects comprehensive planning because planners struggle with information and incentives, keeping markets for goods.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Schweickart says the planet cannot sustain ever more mindless consumption, which does not make people happier, and expects consumerism to diminish under Economic Democracy (s6).

corporate-influence.rationale: The Stanford entry says lobbying has undermined political processes so that market rules benefit large corporations (s5, section 4.2), and Schweickart says the capitalist class dominates the political system (s6).

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Schweickart says the model eliminates basic economic insecurity through full employment, free childcare, health care and education, and a decent retirement income for all (s6), and says poverty would be virtually eliminated.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Rule is by democratic institutions for all, not dictatorial class power.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Workers divide net proceeds themselves in a market economy, so distribution tracks the firm's results, not need.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Schweickart proposes a flat tax on capital assets, not income, and egalitarian goals favour progressive income taxation.

free-basic-services-for-all.rationale: Schweickart's model includes free childcare, free health care and free education as part of eliminating basic economic insecurity (s6, section on special measures for families).

free-economic-experiment.rationale: The model sets out a specific blueprint of worker-run firms, markets and public investment rather than leaving the choice open.

free-trade.rationale: Schweickart says an economic democracy trades freely only with countries of comparable worker incomes and regulations, and otherwise follows 'a policy of fair trade, not free trade' (s6, section on socialist protectionism).

gradual-change.rationale: Schweickart points to the Meidner Plan as a model for gradual, peaceful transition to economic democracy (s6), though he also sketches crisis-driven scenarios.

harm-principle.rationale: Schweickart says people's real freedom to live as they see fit is to be protected so long as they do not harm others, 'in accordance with the harm principle' of Mill (s6, section on liberty).

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Economic democracy removes capital's claim on income and distributes firm proceeds to workers, so income follows work rather than ownership.

job-guarantee.rationale: Schweickart's extended model makes the government the employer of last resort, so that anyone who cannot find work elsewhere is given a low-wage but decent job (s6, section on the employer of last resort).

labour-priority-over-capital.rationale: Ellerman holds that the democratic firm is one where labour hires capital rather than capital hiring labour, and that capitalism is defined by the latter (s9, Chapter 6, The Employer-Employee Relationship).

limit-campaign-donations.rationale: Schweickart says reversing Citizens United would be an important step (s6), and Dahl says limiting the use of money in politics may be needed to protect political equality (s8).

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The model keeps markets for goods but replaces labor and capital markets, so "free markets" as stated is rejected while markets are valued over central planning.

moral-incentives.rationale: Markets and profit sharing supply material incentives, and SEP notes the incentive-duty model is a different Carensian variant.

municipal-property.rationale: In Schweickart's model firms are controlled by their own workers and capital is socially owned, not owned by the local community.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Malleson presents economic democracy as a third path that is 'neither capitalist nor communist' (s7).

night-watchman-state.rationale: The state holds capital, collects the tax and funds public banks, far beyond a night watchman.

one-party-rule.rationale: Democracy is the central theme and Schweickart calls capitalism incompatible with genuine democracy.

participatory-democracy.rationale: The model's core is that people govern their own workplaces, one person one vote, extending democracy beyond politics.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Schweickart says the personal property of individuals should be more secure under Economic Democracy than under capitalism, even though most means of production are collective (s6, section on private property).

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: Schweickart envisages the transition as 'a democratic, nonviolent restructuring of basic economic institutions' (s6, section 3 on principal means).

positive-liberty.rationale: Schweickart says the job security of Economic Democracy enhances the real freedom people have to live as they see fit (s6, section on liberty).

production-for-use.rationale: Markets and profit remain as signals, so production is not organized chiefly by need.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Schweickart ties the capitalist class's income to paying workers less than the value they create, 'i.e., on worker exploitation' (s6, section on labour).

property-franchise.rationale: The case for economic democracy is the extension of equal democratic rights, so wealth-limited voting contradicts its premise.

property-fundamental.rationale: Economic democrats subordinate private property in capital to democratic control, whether by abolition or by a mix circumscribed by democratic laws (s5, section 1.2), and Schweickart restricts private ownership of the means of production and makes large firms saleable only to the state (s6).

public-ownership.rationale: The strands split: Schweickart keeps collective ownership of capital with the state leasing firms to workers (s6), Dahl prefers cooperative ownership to state ownership (s8), and the Stanford entry says some economic democrats want abolition of private ownership of the means of production and others a mix of public and private forms (s5, section 1.2).

racial-franchise.rationale: The model rests on equal democratic citizenship, so a racial limit on voting is contrary to its premise.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Schweickart subjects private and cooperative firms alike to health, safety and environmental regulation (s6), and Malleson describes a 'highly regulated and redistributive market' (s7).

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The central claim is that democracy and economic dynamism are compatible; democratic deficits are the problem.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Schweickart's social tariff rebates proceeds to poorer exporting countries and lets them devote more resources to their own people's needs, and he suggests sharing intellectual property with them (s6).

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Schweickart acknowledges a human obligation to strive to eliminate poverty everywhere, and suggests rich economic democracies share intellectual property and research with poor countries (s6).

say-in-proportion-to-effect.rationale: Hahnel defines economic democracy as decision-making power in proportion to the degree one is affected (s10, Chapter 5), and Wright says he shares this understanding of democracy.

social-market-economy.rationale: Schweickart's model keeps markets for goods and services and includes the welfare services of the Nordic countries (s6, section on government expenditure).

socialized-markets.rationale: Schweickart (s6) and Malleson (s7) combine markets with worker-run enterprises, and Dahl (s8) favours cooperative ownership of self-governing firms. The Stanford entry (s5, section 1.2) notes that Albert and Hahnel dissent in favour of democratic planning, and Schweickart's firms are state-owned and leased to workers.

state-as-business.rationale: The model extends democracy into business, not business logic into government.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Investment is socially controlled through democratically accountable public banks and legislatures set shares, though firms choose projects within it.

state-finances-worker-businesses.rationale: In Schweickart's model all investment funds are allocated by democratically accountable public banks to worker-run enterprises (s6), and Malleson's four pillars include worker cooperatives with finance provided by public banks (s7).

state-harmful.rationale: The model assigns the state roles in holding capital, collecting the tax and funding public banks, and SEP stresses that socialism is not anti-state.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Schweickart's socialist protectionism imposes a social tariff on imports from low-wage or lax-regulation countries to block race-to-the-bottom competition, with the proceeds rebated to the exporting countries (s6).

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Malleson says high taxation would prevent the rich from becoming super-rich (s7), and the Stanford entry says economic democracy is often paired with a call to reduce inequality from above and from below (s5, section 1.2).

taxation-theft.rationale: The model depends on a capital-assets tax as a lease fee for social property.

total-state.rationale: SEP says state control without democratic control is not socialism, and the model is decentralized.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Schweickart ties free trade to comparable worker incomes and social and environmental regulations, and uses a social tariff against countries lacking them (s6), though through tariffs rather than binding agreements.

unions-good.rationale: The Stanford entry describes unions as playing a crucial role in preventing domination of workers, and notes that this has led commentators to argue that democratic states should support them (s5, section 4.2).

universal-healthcare.rationale: Schweickart's Economic Democracy provides free health care, free education and free childcare for all (s6, section on children and families), and says health care need not or should not be subject to market forces.

vanguard-party.rationale: The model rests on workers' own democratic control, not leadership by revolutionaries.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The Stanford entry says economic democracy is seen as a response to the way the economically successful can assemble political power and undermine the fair value of other citizens' political liberties (s5, introduction).

worker-ownership.rationale: Ultimate authority rests with the enterprise's workers, one person one vote; though capital is socially owned and leased, workers collectively control and keep proceeds.

workers-councils.rationale: In Schweickart's model workers' councils govern firms, but long-term economic goals are set by elected national, regional and local legislatures (s6, section on planning).

workplace-democracy.rationale: Workers' democratic control of the firm is the defining feature: Schweickart's worker council elects upper management (s6), Malleson has workers elect managers in cooperatives (s7), and Dahl wants one member, one vote in self-governing enterprises (s8).

missingStatements.text: Firms should be run by their workers, with management chosen by workers' own votes.
missingStatements.rationale: Schweickart's model makes an elected workers' council appoint the chief executive, one person one vote; existing worker-ownership and workplace-democracy statements only partly capture the election of management.

scope: Economic democracy here is the family of proposals, running from the German Wirtschaftsdemokratie of the early twentieth-century union movement to Robert Dahl, David Schweickart, Tom Malleson and David Ellerman, that extend democratic control into the economy: workers govern their firms one person one vote, investment and finance come under democratic public control, and markets are kept only under democratic political control. It includes market-based versions (Schweickart, Malleson, Dahl) and versions that favour democratic planning. It does not cover C. H. Douglas's Social Credit book of the same name, nor co-determination or workplace democracy discussed only as isolated reforms.

name: Wirtschaftsdemokratie
aliases.quote: “Wirtschaftsdemokratie” (“economic democracy”) was used in the German union movement in the early decades of the 20 th century

keyFigures.role: Philosopher whose After Capitalism sets out the best-known model of economic democracy
